'''Julius Ashkin''' (August 23, 1920 – June 4, 1982) was a leader in experimental and theoretical physics known for furthering the evolution of particle physics from nuclear physics. As a theoretical physicist he made contributions in the fields of [[statistical mechanics]], [[Solid-state physics|solid state physics]], [[nuclear physics]], and [[Particle physics|elementary particle physics]]. As an experimental physicist his main contributions concerned the passage of certain particles (pi-mesons, or [[pion]]s) through solid matter and their subsequent decay. He was recognized for the quality of his research and teaching.

== Early life and family ==
Julius Ashkin was born in [[Brooklyn]], New York,<ref name="New York Times">{{cite news |newspaper=[[New York Times]] |date=June 7, 1982 |title=Julius Ashkin, 61, Physicist, Dies |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/06/07/obituaries/julius-ashkin-61-physicist-dies.html |accessdate=April 25, 2016 }}</ref> on August 23, 1920. His parents were Isadore and Anna Ashkin. He had two younger siblings, a brother, [[Arthur Ashkin|Arthur]], also a physicist, and a sister, Ruth. One older sibling, Gertrude, died while young. The family home was in Brooklyn, New York, at 983 E 27 Street. Isadore had immigrated to the United States from [[Odessa]], Ukraine at the age of 19. Anna, five years younger, also came from Ukraine (in her case [[History of the Jews in Galicia (Eastern Europe)|Galicia]]).<ref>"United States Census, 1930," index and images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/pal:/MM9.1.1/X7X3-3YL : accessed December 23, 2013), Isadore Ashkin, Brooklyn (Districts 1251–1500), Kings, New York, United States; citing enumeration district (ED) 1261, sheet, family 298, NARA microfilm publication.</ref><ref>"United States World War I Draft Registration Cards, 1917–1918," index and images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/pal:/MM9.1.1/KXY5-7XY : accessed December 23, 2013), Isadore Ashkin, 1917–1918; citing New York City no 86, New York, United States, NARA microfilm publication M1509, (Washington D.C.: National Archives and Records Administration, n.d); FHL microfilm 001765586.</ref><ref>"United States World War II Draft Registration Cards, 1942," index and images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/pal:/MM9.1.1/F3CQ-T4W : accessed December 23, 2013), Isadore Ashkin, 1942.</ref><ref>"United States Census, 1920," index and images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/pal:/MM9.1.1/MJRV-1VW : accessed December 23, 2013), Isdor Ashkin, Brooklyn Assembly District 18, Kings, New York, United States; citing sheet, family 342, NARA microfilm publication T625, FHL microfilm 1821173.</ref> Within a decade of his landing in New York, Isadore had become a U.S. citizen and was running a dental laboratory at 139 Delancey Street in Manhattan.<ref name=columbiacatalogue /><ref>{{cite book|title=White-Orr's Reference Register|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=S6hRAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA139|year=1918|pages=139–}}</ref> Ashkin's nickname was Julie. He is the uncle of the artist [[Michael Ashkin]].

== Education ==
Ashkin attended Brooklyn's [[James Madison High School (Brooklyn)|James Madison High School]], graduating in 1936, while still a few weeks shy of his 16th birthday. In his senior year, he received honors and awards.<ref name='dailyeagle'>{{cite news | title = Madison High Graduates Told; Rev. Cornelius Greenway Tells Class to Prove School Benefit | date = June 24, 1936 | url = http://www.fultonhistory.com/Newspaper%205/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle%201936%20Grayscale/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle%201936%20%20a%20Grayscale%20-%200891.pdf#xml=http://www.fultonhistory.com/dtSearch/dtisapi6.dll?cmd=getpdfhits&u=ffffffffb66f445e&DocId=7364733&Index=Z%3a\Index%20O-G-T-S&HitCount=12&hits=ce+cf+f6+f7+19b+19c+1b6+1b7+1e9+1ea+1f6+1f7+&SearchForm=C%3a\inetpub\wwwroot\Fulton_New_form.html&.pdf | work = Brooklyn Daily Eagle | page = 30 | accessdate = December 24, 2013}}</ref> He was awarded a scholarship to attend [[Columbia University]],<ref name='dailyeagle1936'>{{cite news | title = 212 From Boro and L.I. Win Scholarships | date = August 28, 1936 | url = http://www.fultonhistory.com/Newspaper%205/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle%201936%20Grayscale/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle%201936%20b%20Grayscale%20-%200143.pdf#xml=http://www.fultonhistory.com/dtSearch/dtisapi6.dll?cmd=getpdfhits&u=ffffffffcb98e927&DocId=7366755&Index=Z%3a\Index%20O-G-T-S&HitCount=2&hits=d0+d1+&SearchForm=C%3a\inetpub\wwwroot\Fulton_New_form.html&.pdf | work = Brooklyn Daily Eagle | page = 26 | accessdate = December 24, 2013}}</ref><ref name='dailyeagleSept36'>{{cite news | title = 8 Pulitzer Price Scholarships Won By Students Here | date = September 18, 1936 | url = http://www.fultonhistory.com/Newspaper%205/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle%201936%20Grayscale/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle%201936%20Grayscale%20-%200789.pdf#xml=http://www.fultonhistory.com/dtSearch/dtisapi6.dll?cmd=getpdfhits&u=ffffffffcef27112&DocId=7370981&Index=Z%3a\Index%20O-G-T-S&HitCount=2&hits=d79+d7a+&SearchForm=C%3a\inetpub\wwwroot\Fulton_New_form.html&.pdf | work = Brooklyn Daily Eagle | page = 3 | accessdate = December 24, 2013}}</ref> where he studied four years as an undergraduate from 1936 to 1940,<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Columbia College Today|url=https://archive.org/details/ldpd_12981092_024|access-date=2020-08-19|website=Internet Archive|page=120|language=en}}</ref> and three as a graduate from 1940 to 1943.<ref name='nierenberg'>{{cite web | url = http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/4797_1.html | title = Interview with Dr. William A. Nierenberg | accessdate = December 7, 2013 | last = Aaserud | first = Finn | date = February 6, 1986 | work = Oral History Transcript | publisher = American Institute of Physics | archive-date = January 12, 2015 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150112072726/http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/4797_1.html | url-status = dead }}</ref>

Physicists then working on Columbia's faculty in those years included professors [[Enrico Fermi]], [[Isidor Isaac Rabi]], [[Hans Bethe]] (visiting), [[Edward Teller]] (visiting), and instructors [[Arnold Nordsieck]], Hugh Paxton,<ref name='paxton'>{{cite journal | title = Hugh Paxton 1909–2003 | journal = Nuclear Criticality Safety Division Newsletter, American Nuclear Society | date = Summer 2004 | pages = 5–6 | url = http://ncsd.ans.org/site/newsletters/2004/summer04.pdf | accessdate = December 9, 2013 | archive-date = February 21, 2014 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140221204630/http://ncsd.ans.org/site/newsletters/2004/summer04.pdf | url-status = dead }}</ref> and [[Willis Lamb]]. All these men were recognized as among the finest of their generation and four of them &mdash; Fermi, Rabi, Bethe, and Lamb &mdash; were to be awarded the Nobel Prize.<ref name='columbiacatalogue'>{{cite journal | title = Catalogue Number for the Sessions of 1941–1942 and 1942–1943 | journal = Catalogue, Columbia University | year = 1940 | url = https://archive.org/details/catalogue1940colu | accessdate = December 8, 2013}}</ref><ref name="Hargittai">{{cite book|author=Istvan Hargittai|title=Judging Edward Teller: A Closer Look at One of the Most Influential Scientists of the Twentieth Century|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XlkmmIHiS9UC&pg=PT505|publisher=Prometheus Books, Publishers|isbn=978-1-61614-269-8|page=140|date=2010-12-31}}</ref>

As an undergraduate, Ashkin was invited to join an honorary mathematics society,<ref name='dailyeagle1938'>{{cite news | title = Honors Upon Us | date = March 13, 1938 | url = http://www.fultonhistory.com/Newspaper%205/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle%201938%20Grayscale/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle%201938%20Grayscale%20-%202121.pdf#xml=http://www.fultonhistory.com/dtSearch/dtisapi6.dll?cmd=getpdfhits&u=ffffffffdd2ae70d&DocId=7388920&Index=Z%3a\Index%20O-G-T-S&HitCount=2&hits=1427+1428+&SearchForm=C%3a\inetpub\wwwroot\Fulton_New_form.html&.pdf | work = Brooklyn Daily Eagle | pages = B7 | accessdate = December 24, 2013}}</ref> and received awards.<ref name= columbiacatalogue /><ref name='putnamprize'>{{cite journal | title = News and Notices | journal = The American Mathematical Monthly | date = May 1940 | volume = 47 | issue = 5 | pages = 300–2| jstor = 2302710 }}</ref><ref name='dailyeagle1940'>{{cite news | title = 73 Boro, L.I. Students in Columbia Class; Among 5,345 Seniors Who Will Get Degrees At 186th Commencement | date = June 5, 1940 | url = http://www.fultonhistory.com/Newspaper%205/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle%201936%20Grayscale/Brooklyn%20NY%20Daily%20Eagle%201936%20%20a%20Grayscale%20-%200891.pdf#xml=http://www.fultonhistory.com/dtSearch/dtisapi6.dll?cmd=getpdfhits&u=ffffffffb66f445e&DocId=7364733&Index=Z%3a\Index%20O-G-T-S&HitCount=12&hits=ce+cf+f6+f7+19b+19c+1b6+1b7+1e9+1ea+1f6+1f7+&SearchForm=C%3a\inetpub\wwwroot\Fulton_New_form.html&.pdf | work = Brooklyn Daily Eagle | page = 30 | accessdate = December 24, 2013}}</ref><ref name='michaelis'>{{cite journal | title = Prizes and Fellowships Academic Honors | journal = Columbia College Bulletin, Columbia University | url = https://www.college.columbia.edu/bulletin/prizes.php | accessdate = December 8, 2013 | archive-date = December 11, 2013 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131211055043/http://www.college.columbia.edu/bulletin/prizes.php | url-status = dead }}</ref> He entered the fall semester as an assistant lecturer and began work toward a master's degree. A year later, having received that degree, he began work toward a Ph.D. under the supervision of Willis Lamb. As a graduate student, Ashkin contributed to one paper in astrophysics.<ref name="AshkinNafe1942">{{cite journal|last1=Ashkin|first1=Julius|last2=Nafe|first2=John E.|last3=Rothstein|first3=Jerome|title=On the Limb Darkening of the Sun.|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|volume=95|year=1942|page=76|doi=10.1086/144375|bibcode = 1942ApJ....95...76A |s2cid=120061330 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and two papers in statistical mechanics<ref name="AshkinLamb1943">{{cite journal|last1=Ashkin|first1=J.|last2=Lamb|first2=W.|title=The Propagation of Order in Crystal Lattices|journal=Physical Review|volume=64|issue=5–6|year=1943|pages=159–178|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.64.159|bibcode = 1943PhRv...64..159A }}</ref><ref name="Niss2004">{{cite journal|last1=Niss|first1=Martin|title=History of the Lenz-Ising Model 1920?1950: From Ferromagnetic to Cooperative Phenomena|journal=Archive for History of Exact Sciences|volume=59|issue=3|year=2004|pages=267–318|doi=10.1007/s00407-004-0088-3|s2cid=122195371 }}</ref><ref name="Schweber1994">{{cite book|author=Silvan S. Schweber|title=QED and the Men who Made it: Dyson, Feynman, Schwinger, and Tomonaga|url=https://archive.org/details/qedmenwhomadeitd0000schw|url-access=registration|year=1994|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-03327-3|pages=[https://archive.org/details/qedmenwhomadeitd0000schw/page/585 585], 669}}</ref><ref name='onsager'>{{cite web | url = http://www.nap.edu/html/biomems/lonsager.pdf | title = Lars Onsager, 1903–1976, a Biographic Memoir | accessdate = December 10, 2013 | last = Longuet-Higgins | first = Christopher |author2=Michael E. Fisher | year = 1991 | publisher = National Academy of Sciences}}</ref><ref name="IllinoisEntwicklungsforschung1992">{{cite book |author1=Lillian Hoddeson Senior Research Physicist University of Illinois |author2=Ernst Braun Senior Research Physicist Institut fur Sozio-Okonomische Entwicklungsforschung |author3=Jurgen Teichmann Senior Research Physicist Deutsches Museum |author4=Spencer Weart Senior Research Physicist Center for History of Physics of the American Institute of Physics |title=Out of the Crystal Maze : Chapters from The History of Solid State Physics: Chapters from The History of Solid State Physics |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WCpPPHhMdRcC |date=11 September 1992|publisher=Oxford University Press, USA |isbn=978-0-19-534532-2}}</ref> He collaborated with Lamb in writing the first of the two papers on statistical mechanics and with Teller in writing the second. This second paper, "Statistics of Two-Dimensional Lattices with Four Components"<ref name=Niss2004 /><ref name=IllinoisEntwicklungsforschung1992 /><ref name="TellerSchoolery2009">{{cite book|author1=Edward Teller|author2=Judith Schoolery|title=Memoirs: A Twentieth Century Journey in Science and Politics|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n82xMo-BI8QC&pg=PA156|date=9 September 2009|publisher=Basic Books|isbn=978-0-7867-5170-9|pages=156–}}</ref><ref name='prola'>{{cite journal | title = Physical Review – September 1943 Volume 64, Issue 5-6 | journal = Physical Review | date = September 1943 | volume = 64 | issue = 5–6 | pages = 178 | url = https://journals.aps.org/pr/issues/64/5-6 | access-date = December 10, 2013 | doi = 10.1103/physrev.64.178 | bibcode = 1943PhRv...64..178A | last1 = Ashkin | first1 = J. | last2 = Teller | first2 = E. | url-access = subscription }}</ref> has since been frequently cited.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://inspirehep.net/record/47289/citations | title = Citations for ''Statistics of Two-Dimensional Lattices with Four Components'' | accessdate = 2014-02-09 }}</ref> He received his Ph.D. in physics in 1943.<ref name='cmu'>{{cite journal | title = About Julius Ashkin | journal = Mellon College of Science Faculty Handbook, Carnegie Mellon University | url = https://www.cmu.edu/mcs/fac_staff/handbook/AshkinBio.html | accessdate = December 7, 2013 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140222193257/http://www.cmu.edu/mcs/fac_staff/handbook/AshkinBio.html | archive-date=February 22, 2014}}</ref><ref name='wolfenstein'>{{cite journal | title = Julius Ashkin | journal = Physics Today | first = Lincoln | last = Wolfenstein | volume = 35 | issue = 8 | page = 66 | doi=10.1063/1.2915225|bibcode = 1982PhT....35h..66W | year = 1982 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

== Manhattan Project ==

=== Early stages of the Manhattan Project at Columbia University===
During the latter part of 1942, before completing his Ph.D. work, Ashkin accepted an offer to work in the [[Manhattan Project]]. Early work on the development of the atom bomb had taken place at Columbia during the six years Ashkin was an undergraduate and graduate student there. When the process of [[nuclear fission]] was discovered in 1938, scientists in many locations in Europe and the United States began intense work to understand and control the phenomenon. Researchers at Columbia and nearby [[Princeton University]] were in the forefront of this work. There's no information on how much, if at all, Ashkin was involved in the effort at this early stage of his career, but it is certain that the Columbia physics department was the workplace for scientists who were devoted to the secret development of a new and phenomenally powerful weapon. These men included men already mentioned &mdash; Fermi, Rabi, Teller, and Bethe &mdash; as well as [[Leó Szilárd]] (who worked with Fermi to demonstrate that a nuclear reaction was possible), [[Herbert L. Anderson]] (then, like Ashkin, a Columbia graduate student), [[John R. Dunning]] (an associate professor at Columbia who had built a small cyclotron in the mid-1930s), [[Walter Zinn]] (a Columbia professor who worked with the Columbia cyclotron to demonstrate the possibility of a sustained chain reaction), [[George B. Pegram]] (Dean of Columbia's Faculties of Political Science, Philosophy, and Pure Science, who helped bring Fermi to the United States and brought him together with representatives of the U.S. Navy Department for the first discussion of the atomic bomb) and [[Harold Urey]] (associate professor of chemistry whose work on separation of isotopes resulted in the discovery of [[deuterium]]).<ref name='nuclearfission'>{{cite web | url = http://www.aip.org/history/acap/topics/fission.jsp | title = Nuclear Fission, 1938–1942 | accessdate = December 9, 2013 | work = Array of Contemporary American Physicists, American Institute of Physics | url-status = dead | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20131024002456/http://www.aip.org/history/acap/topics/fission.jsp | archivedate = October 24, 2013 }}</ref> In addition, Columbia received visits from scientists at Princeton University who were coordinating their work with Columbia colleagues. These included [[John Archibald Wheeler|John Wheeler]], [[Edward Creutz]],<ref name='creutz'>{{cite web | url = https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Creutz_Edward.pdf | title = Edward Chester Creutz, 1913–2009, a Biographical Memoir | access-date = December 8, 2013 | last = Hinman | first = George | year = 2010 | publisher = National Academy of Sciences | url-status = live | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140222054142/http://www.nasonline.org/publications/biographical-memoirs/memoir-pdfs/Creutz_Edward.pdf | archive-date = February 22, 2014 }}</ref> and [[Robert R. Wilson]].<ref name=nuclearfission />

=== Metallurgical Laboratory ===
When Ashkin accepted an invitation to join the Manhattan Project he was still working on his Ph.D. He spent the last few months of 1942 at the [[Metallurgical Laboratory]] at the University of Chicago and then worked at the [[Los Alamos Laboratory]] from mid-1943 to mid-1945. The scientists at the Metallurgical Laboratory, or Met Lab as it was called, used a nuclear reactor called the [[Chicago Pile-1|Chicago Pile]] to produce the world's first controlled chain reaction.<ref name='firstpile'>{{cite web | url = http://www.iaea.org/Publications/Magazines/Bulletin/Bull040su/04005004147su.pdf | title = The First Pile | accessdate = December 26, 2013 | last = Allardice | first = Corbin | author2 = Edward R. Trapnell | publisher = International Atomic Energy Agency | quote = Originally written in 1946, this was the first comprehensive narrative account of the construction and operation of the world's first nuclear reactor. Though popular in approach and style, the story was written after extensive consultations with a number of the scientists directly associated with the great experiment, much of it being constructed from their personal recollections of what happened on 2 December 1942. The account is reprinted here by permission of the United States Atomic Energy Commission. | url-status = dead | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20140221192348/http://www.iaea.org/Publications/Magazines/Bulletin/Bull040su/04005004147su.pdf | archivedate = 21 February 2014 }}</ref> They built the reactor in a disused squash court under the bleachers of Stagg Field, the university's old football stadium. They had been brought together from Columbia and Princeton by [[Arthur Compton]] who was a professor of physics at the University of Chicago. The Met Lab consisted of two divisions. Fermi, Anderson, Zinn, Creutz, and Szilard were key members of the physics division; Bethe and Teller of the theoretical division.<ref name='manhattanacap'>{{cite web | url = http://www.aip.org/history/acap/institutions/manhattan.jsp | title = The Manhattan Project and predecessor organizations | accessdate = December 9, 2013 | work = Array of Contemporary Scientists, American Institute of Physics | url-status = dead | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20121017032813/http://www.aip.org/history/acap/institutions/manhattan.jsp | archivedate = October 17, 2012 }}</ref>

Although Ashkin's interest, experience, and skill would seem to place him with the theoretical division, he worked in the physics division in a group called "Nuclear Physics &mdash; Experimental." His placement in this group suggests that Ashkin had prior experience in carrying out nuclear experiments while a student at Columbia. With the other members of the group &mdash; Feld, Szilard, [[Robert F. Christy]], Herbert E. Kubitschek,<ref name='petition'>{{cite web | url = http://www.dannen.com/decision/45-07-17.html | title = A Petition to the President of the United States | accessdate = December 12, 2013 | author = Leo Szilard| date = July 17, 1945 | work = U.S. National Archives, Record Group 77, Records of the Chief of Engineers, Manhattan Engineer District, Harrison-Bundy File, folder #76|display-authors=etal}}</ref> and [[Seymour Bernstein (1909-1981)|Seymour Bernstein]] (untraced) &mdash; Ashkin produced a number of technical reports on the theoretical aspects of nuclear fission.<ref name="AshkinBernstein1947">{{cite book|author1=J. Ashkin|author2=S. Bernstein|author3=B. Feld|author4=H. Kubitschek |author5=L. Szilard, University of Chicago, U.S. Atomic Energy Commission|title=Preliminary comparison of radon-boron and radium-beryllium neutron sources|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vmsJ6utV7E8C|year=1947|publisher=Technical Information Division, Oak Ridge Operations}}</ref><ref name='activation'>{{cite journal | title = Activation of Fast Neutron Detectors by Cyclotron and by Fission Neutrons | journal = Technical Report CF-863 Metallurgical Lab University of Chicago | date = April 1, 1943 | first = Julius | last = Ashkin |author2=B. T. Feld | osti = 4371153 }}</ref><ref name="SzilardBernstein1948">{{cite journal|last1=Szilard|first1=L.|last2=Bernstein|first2=S.|last3=Feld|first3=B.|last4=Ashkin|first4=J.|title=Inelastic Scattering of Fast Neutrons by Fe, Pb, and Bi|journal=Physical Review|volume=73|issue=11|year=1948|pages=1307–1310|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.73.1307|bibcode = 1948PhRv...73.1307S }}</ref><ref name="Wigner2001">{{cite book|author=Eugene Paul Wigner|author-link=Eugene Wigner|title=Historical and Biographical Reflections and Syntheses|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Dn4zVoy6QeAC&pg=PA148|year=2001|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3-540-57294-7|pages=148–149}}</ref> With Feld, he also produced a practical report on ''Poisoning and Production in a Power Plant'' which considered the power potential of sustained nuclear reactions as well as the radiation poisoning and other hazards that accompanied them. All these reports were secret when produced and have since been declassified and released.<ref name="SzilardBernstein1948"/><ref name='poisoning'>{{cite journal | title = Poisoning and Production in a Power Plant | journal = Technical Report CP-381; A-416 Metallurgical Lab, University of Chicago | date = December 15, 1942 | first1 = Julius | last1 = Ashkin | first2 = R.F. |last2=Christy |first3=B.T. |last3=Feld | osti = 4354650 }}</ref>

=== Los Alamos ===
At Los Alamos Ashkin was assigned to work in the Theoretical Division headed by Bethe. There were five groups in this division and Ashkin was assigned to group 4, Diffusion Problems. His responsibilities, broadly, permitted him to build upon work he had done as a graduate student and in his months at Met Lab. T-4's group leader was [[Richard Feynman]]; Ashkin was alternate leader. The initial members were Richard Ehrich,<ref name='ehrlich'>{{cite news | title = Dr. Richard Ehrich, Obituary | date = January 31, 2002 | work = Daily Gazette, Gainesville, Florida }}</ref> and [[Frederick Reines]]. {{Interlanguage link|Theodore Welton|de}} joined it in the early spring of 1944.<ref name=Schweber1994 /><ref name='welton'>{{cite news | title = Theodore Allen Welton, Obituary | date = November 23, 2010 | url = http://www.oakridger.com/article/20101123/NEWS/311239994 | work = OakRidger, Oak Ridge, Tennessee | accessdate = December 13, 2013}}</ref> The group's main task was to estimate the rate at which neutrons would diffuse through the explosive core of the bomb during nuclear fission. Somewhat facetiously Feynman later claimed that the work done at Los Alamos was mostly engineering, not science.<ref name='losalamosfrombelow'>{{cite journal | title = Los Alamos From Below: Reminiscences 1943–1945 | journal = Engineering and Science, California Institute of Technology | date = January–February 1976 | first = Richard | last = Feynman | volume = 39 | issue = 2 }}</ref> Welton, however, told of the group's long hard hours, high spirits and cohesiveness, and said they achieved some excellent successes in theoretical physics.<ref name="Welton2007">{{cite journal|last1=Welton|first1=Theodore A.|title=Memories of Feynman|journal=Physics Today|volume=60|issue=2|year=2007|pages=46–52|doi=10.1063/1.2711636|bibcode = 2007PhT....60b..46W }}</ref><ref name='marshakoral'>{{cite web | url = http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/4760_2.html | title = Oral History Transcript — Dr. Robert E. Marshak, conducted by Dr. Charles Weiner at Professor Marshak's Office, University of Rochester, Rochester, New York, June 16, 1970, Center for History of Physics of the American Institute of Physics | accessdate = December 21, 2013 | date = June 16, 1970 | work = American Institute of Physics | quote = You see, we were so busy&nbsp;... Those were rather brief years - for me almost two, for others three. The maximum time I guess, was about three and a quarter years. And these were very intense years. One really concentrated completely on the war work and trying to get that bomb built before the Germans. }}</ref> Their work required a great number of mathematical computations, which, Welton remembered, they performed using Work Projects Administration math tables and big Marchant mechanical calculators. In fact, their assistant, an enlisted man named Murray Peshkin, remembered the group as having an unending need for calculation. An undergraduate with a major in physics at the time he was recruited, he was put, as he recalled, "to solving differential equations that were needed to predict the critical mass of a bomb under various assumptions about the many unknown properties of the nuclei in the bomb material."<ref name='peshkin'>{{cite news | first = Murray | last = Peshkin | title = To Be Young, Gifted and Building The Bomb | date = June 24, 2005 | url = https://www.chicagotribune.com/2005/07/24/to-be-young-gifted-and-building-the-bomb/ | work = Chicago Tribune | access-date = December 7, 2013}}</ref>

Security at Los Alamos was very tight by standards of the time. The site was an uninhabited desert location (formerly a private school) whose perimeter was fenced, with guards at the gates. The scientists were permitted outside the facility but there was little available transportation. (Since they were not members of the military, they could not be ordered to comply with military secrecy orders and instead voluntarily agreed to abide by them.)<ref name=losalamosfrombelow /><ref name='espionageenclyclopedia'>{{cite encyclopedia | url = http://www.faqs.org/espionage/Lo-Mo/Manhattan-Project.html | title = Manhattan Project | accessdate = December 15, 2013 | last = Lerner | first = BrendaWilmoth | encyclopedia = Espionage Encyclopedia}}</ref><ref name='fuller'>{{cite web | url = http://science.howstuffworks.com/manhattan-project3.htm | title = Manhattan Project Organization | accessdate = December 15, 2013 | last = Fuller | first = John | work = How the Manhattan Project Worked | date = 17 January 2008 | publisher = How Stuff Works}}</ref><ref name='cid'>{{cite book | editor-last1 = Rafalko | editor-first1 = Frank J. | title = A Counter Intelligence Reader | chapter = Security and the Los Alamos Project | volume = II | publisher = U.S. National Counterintelligence Center | chapter-url = http://www.fas.org/irp/ops/ci/docs/ci2/2ch1_f.htm | accessdate = December 15, 2013}}</ref> Although urban-raised scientists, like Ashkin, were far from the amusements that cities afford, they were able to find amusing things to do. It helped that some of the married ones were able to bring their wives to live in the town of Los Alamos and thus parties of men and women could get together for social activities. These include such things as hikes of hills and canyons of the surrounding wilderness areas. It's likely Ashkin played outdoor team sports while at Los Alamos. A Met Lab colleague remembered playing touch football with him and Feld on an open space called the midway at the University of Chicago.<ref name='agnew'>{{cite journal | title = Early Impressions | journal = Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists | first = Harold M. | last = Agnew | volume = 38 | issue = 10 | pages = 20–21 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jwoAAAAAMBAJ&pg=PP1 |date=December 1982| accessdate = December 21, 2013 | quote = After being associated for 40 years with our nation's nuclear program it's difficult to select a particular incident which stands out above others. It may bemuse my colleagues to know what events I do not choose to write about on this occasion: events such as being with Enrico Fermi on December 2, 1942 under Staff Field; or being over Hiroshima on August 6, 1945; or playing touch football with Bernie Feld and the ''real'' Julius Ashkin (as opposed to the imposter who used Ashkin's name) on the Chicago Midway; or making a one-gram radium beryllium source on an afternoon in New York, putting it in a briefcase, and flying back to Chicago with it under my seat.| bibcode = 1982BuAtS..38j..20A | doi = 10.1080/00963402.1982.11455818 | url-access = subscription }}</ref>

Feynman was particularly adept at leavening hard work with light-hearted games. His genius was as much playful as serious. He took pride in deceiving the mail censors, guessing the combinations of safes in which secret files were stored, picking door locks, and teasing the guards (he would depart from the main gate, circle around the perimeter to a hole in the fence, re-enter the facility, and then exit the gate again, thus causing confusion and consternation both.) He also liked to pound his bongo drums, a practice which made those within hearing range grit their teeth but which he believed put him in touch with the spirits of the Indians who formerly inhabited the place. Feynman wasn't unusual in his affection for drumming but his choice of musical genres was atypical as was his lack of skill as a drummer.<ref name='music'>{{cite journal | title = Is it the mystery, or the structure, or the discipline? Whatever the reason, playing music seems to attract physicists | journal = Cornell Chronicle | date = August 10, 2006 | first = Lauren | last = Gold | url = https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2006/08/cornell-physicists-face-music-and-love-it | access-date = December 16, 2013}}</ref> It appears that the music produced by his friends offended him as much as his relentless noise offended them. When Ashkin played the recorder, Feynman said he was using "an infernally popular wooden tube ... for making noises bearing a one-one correspondence to black dots on a piece of paper -- in imitation to music."<ref>{{cite book |title=Genius: The Life and Science of Richard Feynman |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IWQ_y90P2uIC |year=1992 |publisher=Vintage Books |isbn=978-0-679-74704-8 | page=191}}</ref>

In 1946, before the scientists at Los Alamos dispersed, there was a brief period during which they gave lectures on subjects in which they had expertise. The program was styled the "Los Alamos University" and some junior members of laboratory personnel received college credit for attending them. Ashkin's were on theoretical mechanics.<ref name='losalamosuniversity'>{{cite journal | title = Technical Report AECU-167; (M-4297) | journal = United States Office of Scientific and Technical Information | first1 = Julius | last1 = Ashkin | first2 = J. |last2=Keller |first3=C. |last3=Richman }}</ref> The course description says it covered the dynamics of particles, rigid bodies, elastic media, and fluids using vector analysis, particle dynamics, Lagrange's equations, and Hamilton's equations.<ref name='truslow'>{{cite book | last1 = Truslow | first1 = Edith C. | last2 = Smith | first2 = Ralph Carlisle | title = Manhattan District History: Project Y, the Los Alamos Project, Volume 2: August 1945 through December 1946 | publisher = Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory | date = 1961 <!--release date--> | url = http://www.osti.gov/manhattan-project-history/publications/LANLMDHProjectYPart2.pdf | accessdate = December 14, 2013 | quote = A part of the Manhattan District History commissioned by Leslie R. Groves.}}</ref>

Along with other members of the Feynman team, Ashkin produced technical reports while at Los Alamos. These were classified at the time but have since been made public. One example gives an idea of the work carried out by the group. It is ''The Calculation of Critical Masses Including the Effects of the Distribution of Neutron Energies'', by Feynman, R.P.; Welton, T.A.; Ashkin, J.; Ehrlich, R.; Peshkin, M.; and Reines, F. Report LA-524(Del.) January 21, 1947 (extract from abstract: "Convenient approximate methods are developed for the calculation of critical sizes and multiplication rates of spherical, active cores surrounded by infinite tampers. Special attention is given to those problems arising from the fact that neutrons of different velocities have different properties. The methods consist essentially of approximating the neutron densities at each velocity by fundamental mode shapes for each velocity.")<ref name='criticalmasses'>{{cite journal | title = The Calculation of Critical Masses Including the Effects of the Distribution of Neutron Energies | journal = Technical Report LA-524(Del.), los Alamos Scientific Lab., N. Mex. | date = January 21, 1947 | first = Richard | last = Feynman |display-authors=etal}}</ref>

On July 16, 1945, Ashkin was present at the first-ever explosion of a nuclear bomb at the [[Trinity (nuclear test)|Trinity test site]], Alamogordo. Only a few of the many scientists were permitted to witness this unspeakably dramatic culmination of their work. Ashkin was probably there because of his work on radiation poisoning, begun at Met Lab and probably continued afterward.<ref name= poisoning />

In 1950 it was revealed that one of the scientists at Los Alamos, [[Klaus Fuchs]], was providing the Soviet intelligence bureau, [[NKGB]], with secret information about bomb research. Between 1943 and 1946, Fuchs worked at both Columbia and Los Alamos. When the FBI interviewed Bethe and Feynman about their relationship with Fuchs while at Los Alamos, Feynman said Fuchs was quiet, reserved and not inclined to mix with other scientists outside of work. He also said he believed Fuchs was less stand-offish with Ashkin and seemed friendly with him.<ref name='fuchs'>{{cite web | url = http://vault.fbi.gov/rosenberg-case/klaus-fuchs/klaus-fuchs-part-62-of | title = FBI Records - Klaus Fuchs - Part 6, Interviews with Associates of Fuchs | accessdate = December 21, 2013 | date = June 1950 | quote = Feynman recalled that he believes Fuchs was friendly at Los Alamos with Dr. Julius Ashkin who is presently at the University of Rochester, Rochester, New York, and with Robert Eugene Marshak and his wife Ruth.}}</ref>

== Academic positions ==

=== University of Rochester ===
On leaving Los Alamos in 1946 Ashkin obtained a position as assistant professor at the University of Rochester and in 1950 he moved to the Carnegie Institute of Technology (later Carnegie Mellon University). He remained at CMU for the rest of his life, serving as professor and for a period head of the physics department. [[Robert Marshak]] brought Ashkin to the University of Rochester in 1946. As an assistant professor he taught mechanics and thermodynamics and theoretical physics and performed pioneering experiments on neutron-proton, proton-proton, and nucleon-nucleon scattering.<ref name=wolfenstein /><ref name=marshakoral /><ref name='goldberg'>{{cite web | url = http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/34461.html | title = Interview with Dr. Joshua Goldberg at Caltech University | accessdate = December 7, 2013 | last = Rickles | first = Dean | date = March 21, 2011 | work = Oral History Transcript | publisher = American Institute of Physics}}</ref><ref name="AshkinWu1948">{{cite journal|last1=Ashkin|first1=Julius|last2=Wu|first2=Ta-You|title=Neutron-Proton and Proton-Proton Scattering at High Energies|journal=Physical Review|volume=73|issue=9|year=1948|pages=973–985|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.73.973|bibcode = 1948PhRv...73..973A }}</ref><ref name="WuAshkin1948">{{cite journal|last1=Wu|first1=Ta-YOU|last2=Ashkin|first2=Julius|title=Elastic and Inelastic Scattering of 100- to 200-Mev Protons or Neutrons by Deuterons|journal=Physical Review|volume=73|issue=9|year=1948|pages=986–1001|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.73.986|bibcode = 1948PhRv...73..986W }}</ref><ref name="AshkinMarshak1949">{{cite journal|last1=Ashkin|first1=J.|last2=Marshak|first2=R.|title=Bremsstrahlung in High Energy Nucleon-Nucleon Collisions|journal=Physical Review|volume=76|issue=1|year=1949|pages=58–60|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.76.58|bibcode = 1949PhRv...76...58A }}</ref>

While at Rochester, Ashkin was the first scientist to formally recognize the importance of the [[Feynman diagram]]. Feynman devised the diagram in 1948 to provide a simple visualization of the mathematical expressions governing the behavior of subatomic particles. Although the diagram and its offshoots were later seen as extremely important tools, Feynman did not give them a theoretical framework nor did he explain how he proposed they be used. Physicists had difficulty in understanding their function, distrusted their simplicity, and were reluctant to give them formal recognition. Feynman later said physicists did not realize the diagram's power and would employ a more complex method created by [[Julian Schwinger]]. Ashkin, he said, was the first to break with this pattern: "They somehow or other couldn’t do it. They had to go through this [the Schwinger method] to believe it. But that's all right. The only person who didn't, the first paper where it was used directly — which I kept looking for, I kept flipping through the [[Physical Review]] as it came out — was Ashkin. He'd done some calculation for some experiment, and he said, 'We’ve calculated this using Feynman's rules.' Bloop! There it was in writing! Then gradually more and more people did it."<ref name='feynmanaip'>{{cite web | url = http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/5020_4.html | title = Interview with Dr. Richard Feynman at Altadena, CA | accessdate = December 7, 2013 | last = Weiner | first = Charles | date = June 28, 1966 | work = Oral History Transcript | publisher = American Institute of Physics}}</ref><ref name="Kaiser2005A">{{cite journal |last1=Kaiser |first1=David |title=Physics and Feynman's Diagrams |journal=American Scientist |volume=93 |issue=2 |year=2005 |page=156 |doi=10.1511/2005.2.156}}</ref><ref name="Kaiser2005B">{{cite book |author=David Kaiser |title=Pedagogy and the Practice of Science: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qqqQ8pTdxfEC |year=2005 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-11288-8}}</ref><ref name="Kaiser2009">{{cite book|author=David Kaiser|title=Drawing Theories Apart: The Dispersion of Feynman Diagrams in Postwar Physics |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_wz9JZvBt78C&pg=PA220 |date=November 15, 2009 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0-226-42265-7 |pages=220–}}</ref>

While he was teaching at the University of Rochester, Ashkin married Claire Ruderman, a biologist studying at the same university.<ref name="Ashkin1947">{{cite book|author=Claire Ruderman Ashkin|title=A Contribution to the Knowledge of Stridulating Organs in Spiders|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aJC2tgAACAAJ|year=1947|publisher=University of Rochester. Department of Biology.}}</ref><ref name="Science1948">{{cite book |author=American Association for the Advancement of Science |title=Summarized Proceedings ... and a Directory of Members |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zWIbAAAAMAAJ |year=1948 |publisher=The Association}}</ref> The couple had two daughters, Beth and Laura.<ref name="New York Times"/>

=== Carnegie Mellon University ===
In 1950 Ashkin joined the physics faculty of Carnegie Mellon University (then the Carnegie Institute of Technology) where Edward Creutz was department head and director of a new 450 MeV proton synchrocyclotron that CIT had built in nearby Saxonburg, Pennsylvania.<ref name=wolfenstein/><ref name=creutz/> Joining fellow scientists [[Lincoln Wolfenstein]] and Sergio de Benedetti,<ref name='debenedetti'>{{cite journal | title = Sergio DeBenedetti--1912–1994 | journal = Inter-Actions, Department of Physics, Carnegie Mellon University | year = 1995 | url = http://www.cmu.edu/physics/news/newsletter/interactions1995.pdf | accessdate = December 8, 2013 | url-status = dead | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20140222193246/http://www.cmu.edu/physics/news/newsletter/interactions1995.pdf | archivedate = February 22, 2014 }}</ref> at this time Ashkin began to transition from mainly theoretical to mainly experimental work. The cyclotron remained in use at the Saxonburg Nuclear Research Center until the mid-1970s when it was dismantled and, using it, Ashkin was able to produce some of his best-known experimental results.<ref name="Steinberger2005">{{cite book |author=J. Steinberger |title=Learning About Particles - 50 Privileged Years |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zgyotyvu_eQC |year=2005 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-21329-1 | quote = The groundwork for the understanding of this resonance was done by Fermi and coworkers at the slightly higher energy Chicago cyclotron, which began to function in 1951. It was more definitively established by Ashkin and coworkers, using a yet slightly higher energy cyclotron at Carnegie Institute of Technology, which came into operation in 1953.... Fermi could almost reach it and Ashkin could finally see it clearly. (p. 53) }}</ref><ref name='saxonburg'>{{cite journal | title = Saxonburg Cyclotron 50th Reunion | journal = Inter-Actions, Department of Physics, Carnegie Mellon University | first = John | last = Fetkovich | year = 1997 | url = http://www.cmu.edu/physics/news/newsletter/interactions1997.pdf | accessdate = December 8, 2013 | archive-date = February 22, 2014 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140222193236/http://www.cmu.edu/physics/news/newsletter/interactions1997.pdf | url-status = dead }}</ref>

In 1953, with Bethe, his former director of theoretical work in Los Alamos, Ashkin published an article closely related to the work they had then done. This article, "Passage of Radiations Through Matter," summarized the effects of particles and radiation as they passed through solids.<ref name="Segrè1953">{{cite book|author=Emilio Segrè|title=Experimental Nuclear Physics, Vol. I|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ox9RAAAAMAAJ|year=1953|publisher=John Wiley|isbn=9780598745040 }}</ref> In time it became a standard reference for physics experimenters.<ref name=wolfenstein/><ref name="L'Annunziata2007">{{cite book |author=Michael F. L'Annunziata |title=Radioactivity: Introduction and History: Introduction and History |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YpEiPPFlNAAC |date=August 23, 2007 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-054888-3 | quote = Hans Bethe (1933) and Bethe and Ashkin (1953) derived the formula for calculating the stopping power resulting from coulombic interactions of heavy charged particles... }}</ref> Using the CIT cyclotron and following on work done by Bethe and Robert E. Marshak, Ashkin conducted experiments to determine the characteristics of a short-lived particle &mdash; the pi-meson or [[pion]] &mdash; that is produced when high energy cosmic ray protons and other cosmic ray components interact with matter in the Earth's atmosphere.<ref name=wolfenstein/><ref name=marshakoral /><ref name="AshkinSimon1950">{{cite journal |last1=Ashkin |first1=J.|last2=Simon |first2=A. |last3=Marshak |first3=R. |title=On the Scattering of pi-Mesons by Nucleons |journal=Progress of Theoretical Physics |volume=5 |issue=4 |year=1950 |pages=634–668 |doi=10.1143/ptp/5.4.634|bibcode=1950PThPh...5..634A |doi-access=free }}</ref> Ashkin served as chair of the physics department between 1961 and 1972.<ref name=cmu /> After he died, CMU created the ''Julius Ashkin Teaching Award'' in his honor.<ref name='award'>{{cite journal | title = Mellon College of Science -- Julius Ashkin Teaching Award | journal = Faculty Handbook, Mellon College of Science, Carnegie Mellon University | year = 1988 | url = http://www.cmu.edu/mcs/fac_staff/handbook/ashkin.html | accessdate = December 7, 2013 | archive-date = September 28, 2013 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130928104929/http://www.cmu.edu/mcs/fac_staff/handbook/ashkin.html | url-status = dead }}</ref>

=== Sabbatical at CERN ===
In 1958–1959 Ashkin won a Ford Foundation grant to spend a sabbatical year in Geneva, Switzerland, at [[CERN]], the European Organization for Nuclear Research.<ref name='fordcern'>{{citation | contribution = Guest Professors | title = Fifth Meeting, Scientific Policy Committee, European Organization for Nuclear Research | date = October 12, 1956 | contribution-url = https://cds.cern.ch/record/1263116/files/CM-P00094814-e.pdf | accessdate = December 7, 2013}}</ref> There, he became a member of the first group of scientists to use that institution's new 600 MeV synchrocyclotron.<ref name='cern1957'>{{cite web | url = http://home.web.cern.ch/about/accelerators/synchrocyclotron | title = The Synchrocyclotron | accessdate = December 7, 2013 | publisher = CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research}}</ref> Using this [[particle accelerator]] he helped to make a significant discovery which confirmed an aspect of the V-A Theory of weak interactions.<ref name='v-a'>{{cite web | url = http://quest.ph.utexas.edu/sudarshan_vminusa.html | title = V-A: Universal Theory of Weak Interaction | accessdate = December 7, 2013 | year = 2006 | work = Seven Science Quests Symposium}}</ref><ref name="AshkinFazzini1959">{{cite journal|last1=Ashkin|first1=J.|last2=Fazzini |first2=T.|last3=Fidecaro|first3=G.|last4=Merrison|first4=A. W.|last5=Paul |first5=H.|last6=Tollestrup|first6=A. V.|title=The electron decay mode of the pion |journal=Il Nuovo Cimento|volume=13|issue=6|year=1959|pages=1240–1262 |doi=10.1007/BF02725130|bibcode=1959NCim...13.1240A|s2cid=14367520 }}</ref><ref name="Ashkin1959">{{cite journal |last1=Ashkin |first1=J .|title=Pion-nucleon scattering |journal=Il Nuovo Cimento |volume=14 |issue=S2 |year=1959 |pages=221–241 |doi=10.1007/BF02913290|bibcode=1959NCim...14S.221A |s2cid=121462503 }}</ref><ref name="AshkinFazzini1960">{{cite journal |last1=Ashkin |first1=J. |last2=Fazzini |first2=T. |last3=Fidecaro |first3=G. |last4=Goldschmidt-Clermont |first4=Y. |last5=Lipman |first5=N. H .|last6=Merrison |first6=A. W. |last7=Paul |first7=H. |title=A new measurement of the mean life of the positive pion |journal=Il Nuovo Cimento |volume=16 |issue=3 |year=1960 |pages=490–504 |doi=10.1007/BF02731913|bibcode=1960NCim...16..490A |s2cid=121823568 }}</ref> Supported by a grant from the Guggenheim Foundation, in 1968 he also spent a year as a Fellow at [[All Souls College, Oxford]].<ref name='guggenheim'>{{cite web | url = http://www.gf.org/fellows/all?index=a&page=11 | title = All Fellows, John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation | accessdate = December 22, 2013}}</ref>

Ashkin died at [[University of Pittsburgh Medical Center#UPMC Montefiore|Montefiore Hospital]] in Pittsburgh, Pennslylvania on June 4, 1982, after a lengthy illness.<ref name="New York Times"/><ref name="cmu"/>
